The earliest stages of life in the Little greenbul (Eurillas virens) are marked by a brief dependency on endogenous resources. Upon hatching, the nestling emerges from an incubated bird egg at a remarkably small size, with the initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick recorded at 2.4 grams [Ww0 = 2.4 grams]. This modest mass demands intensive parental brooding and feeding in the first days following the trophic switch. The incubation period itself, leading to this hatchling event, has been documented under controlled laboratory conditions. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] were observed to complete development and hatch after precisely 13 days [ab = 13 days], a developmental duration that aligns closely with incubation periods reported for other small-bodied Pycnonotidae. This relatively short incubation interval underscores the rapid embryogenesis typical of many passerines inhabiting warm, stable lowland forests. The nestling growth phase that follows is correspondingly swift, characterized by a rapid increase in feather development and musculoskeletal maturation.

As the nestling progresses through the feather-growing nestling stage, a crucial developmental milestone is the achievement of flight capability and departure from the nest. Under the species' typical active metabolic thermal conditions, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestling reaches the fledging stage after a precise interval. Field observations indicate that the time since birth at fledging is 11.5 days [tx = 11.5 days] at this stable body temperature. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This rapid nest departure is an adaptation to high predation pressure within the dense understory of African tropical forests, where prolonged occupancy of a fixed nest site greatly increases mortality risk. Once the fledgling leaves the nest, it remains dependent on its parents for provisioning for several additional weeks. This post-fledging care period is critical, as the immature bird must refine its foraging skills and develop the flight proficiency necessary for independent survival. The plumage of the fledgling gradually transitions from the cryptic downy covering of the chick to the olive-green and yellow-vented adult-like feathering characteristic of the species.

Following nutritional independence and the completion of somatic growth, the juvenile bird enters its first year of life with a series of physiological transitions. Sexual maturation, a process driven by hormonal changes including a testosterone surge in males, culminates in the attainment of reproductive capability. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which represents the core body temperature during active periods, puberty is reached at 39 days since birth [tp = 39 days since birth]. This rapid onset of gonadal maturation is relatively early compared to other African passerines of similar adult body size, and it suggests a life-history strategy favoring early breeding in a relatively aseasonal equatorial environment. However, the attainment of physiological puberty does not coincide with immediate breeding. In many young greenbuls, there is a lag between reaching a sexually mature condition and actually initiating a first clutch, as the individual must secure a territory and accumulate sufficient energetic reserves to support the demands of reproduction. This extended pre-breeding period is reflected in the species' age at first brood.

The timing of the first successful reproductive event for Eurillas virens has been documented in long-term field studies of color-banded populations. The age at first brood, calculated from the time since birth, occurs at approximately 474.5 days since birth [tR = approximately 474.5 days since birth] under a stable environmental temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This significant delay between reaching puberty and initiating a first brood highlights the substantial costs associated with territory establishment and mate acquisition in this species. Once a female does commence breeding, her annual reproductive output is constrained. Field records show that females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and the species raises a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually]. This modest reproductive rate is typical of many forest passerines that provide extended biparental care to their altricial young. The energetic demands of producing and incubating two relatively large eggs, followed by feeding rapidly growing nestlings, likely preclude a second brood within the same breeding season.

Long-term survival and metabolic performance are key metrics that define the life-history pace of the Little greenbul. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been recorded at 3650 days [am = 3650 days] for individuals inhabiting stable, protected forest reserves at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a passerine of its size and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by low annual reproductive output and high adult survival, placing Eurillas virens among the longer-lived members of the Pycnonotidae. Supporting this relatively slow pace of life is the species' resting metabolic rate. Respirometry trials conducted on inactive, post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] measured a basal oxygen consumption of 59.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 59.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is close to the predicted allometric value for a 26-gram passerine, reflecting the standard energetic demands of thermoregulation and tissue maintenance. In terms of sexual size dimorphism, adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 26.1 grams [Wwi = 26.1 grams], whereas males are slightly heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 28.5 grams [Wwi = 28.5 grams]. This modest difference in mass likely relates to differences in competitive or display behaviors.
